Title: The decision you'd remake
Detail_lesson: Most teams carry one decision that quietly shaped everything that came after it. It is rarely the dramatic one; it is usually the quick call made in a corridor or a crowded meeting.
CustomInstruction: Name the decision in one sentence. Then name the single piece of information that would have changed it. Do not relitigate the outcome - identify the missing input.

Title: Reversible or one-way?
Detail_lesson: Some decisions can be undone in an afternoon. Others set concrete: contracts, data models, public commitments. Teams often apply the same amount of deliberation to both.
CustomInstruction: Pick a decision your team is facing right now and estimate the cost of undoing it - in days, money, or trust. Then say whether the current level of debate matches that cost.

Title: Who actually decides?
Detail_lesson: Ownership tends to be clear on the org chart and murky in the room. The gap shows up as decisions that get made twice, or not at all.
CustomInstruction: Describe one recurring decision and name the role - not the person - that should own it. Then say what would visibly change if that ownership were written down.

Title: The risk we stopped discussing
Detail_lesson: Every team has a risk it has quietly accepted. Acceptance is a legitimate choice; forgetting you made it is not.
CustomInstruction: Name a risk your team lives with. Say roughly when it was last discussed out loud, and what event would force it back onto the agenda.

Title: Cheapest way to be wrong
Detail_lesson: The value of an experiment is not what it proves - it is how quickly and cheaply it can disprove something you already believe.
CustomInstruction: Describe the smallest test that would show your current plan is wrong. Give its cost in days and who would have to stop what they are doing.

Title: What would have to be true?
Detail_lesson: Plans rest on assumptions that feel like facts because everyone repeats them. Naming one out loud usually changes the conversation.
CustomInstruction: Take a plan you personally support and state one assumption it depends on. Phrase it as a claim someone could check, not as a hope.

Title: The last thing you declined
Detail_lesson: Declining well is a skill, and the wording matters more than the decision. Most of us default to a phrase we have never examined.
CustomInstruction: Describe something you turned down and quote the sentence you used, as closely as you remember it. Judge the sentence, not the decision.

Title: Work nobody would start today
Detail_lesson: Effort keeps flowing to things that made sense eighteen months ago. Stopping them requires someone with the standing to say so.
CustomInstruction: Name work still running that nobody would begin today. Then identify what keeps it alive: sunk cost, an outside promise, or simply no one empowered to stop it.

Title: Your cost of yes
Detail_lesson: Every yes displaces something. The displaced thing is usually invisible because it was never scheduled in the first place.
CustomInstruction: Identify what actually slipped the last time you said yes. Name the specific piece of work, not a general feeling of being busy.

Title: The near miss nobody logged
Detail_lesson: Organisations record failures and celebrate successes. The most instructive events - the ones caught just in time - usually leave no trace.
CustomInstruction: Describe a problem that was caught late but not too late. Then say whether it was caught by a process or by an individual paying attention, and be honest about which.

Title: Surprise, not failure
Detail_lesson: A surprise is cheaper than a failure and carries the same information. Teams that track surprises learn faster than teams that only track incidents.
CustomInstruction: Name something that genuinely surprised your team recently, good or bad. Then state the belief that surprise corrected.

Title: The lesson that didn't stick
Detail_lesson: Retrospective actions have a short half-life. They survive the meeting and rarely survive the next busy week.
CustomInstruction: Recall a retrospective action that quietly died. Say what would have made it survive: an owner, a date, a default, or a smaller scope.
